en.title: The Video Games And More You Should Play This Weekend – September 4, 2026
en.description: Welcome to September 2026, which will forever be known as pre-pre-GTA VI month. Alternatively, it might be known as the month when every single vid...
en.fullContent:
Welcome to September 2026, which will forever be known as pre-pre-GTA VI month. Alternatively, it might be known as the month when every single video game came out. We're already feeling the weight of the September gaming waterfall, but the water is invigorating, if a bit intense. We have lots of game recommendations below (and we didn't even cover everything this week, frankly), but before we get to that, here are some of our biggest stories of the week.

Remember that old samurai Onimusha series from the early 2000s that was basically Resident Evil with swords, and it was really cool and something you may or may not have played at your friends’ house because your parents wouldn’t buy it for you because of demons and blood? Well, guess what: it’s back. Onimusha: Way of the Sword is the first new Onimusha game from Capcom in over two decades, and after covering it all month long for Game Informer’s cover story hub, I’m happy to report that the final game is absolutely worth your time and money. The combat is incredible – challenging, intricate, complex, and constantly building on itself. The characters and setting are good fun, too, and though it has more repetition in its combat arena design than I’d prefer, you still get to kill stuff with protagonist Musashi’s sword… and that’s always a great time. It’s out today, and you can read my Onimusha: Way of the Sword review while it’s downloading. Oh, and if you’re worried about difficulty, don’t be: Onimusha: Way of the Sword has an incredible easy mode.

I was optimistic about The Blood of Dawnwalker after reading my coworker Brian Shea's articles from his cover story trip, but I was still very surprised by how much I like the game. You play as Coen, a Dawnwalker (which means you're a vampire by night and a human by day) who has 30 days to save his family from an evil vampire lord. Each quest you complete advances the clock by a little, and you only have a limited amount of time before the game concludes, which means you have to pick and choose your missions carefully. What I didn't realize until playing, however, is that there's no main quest – you choose what feels important to you in your journey to save your loved ones. It's an incredibly empowering combination, and I really feel like my decisions matter when I focus on a quest to reforge an ancient sword instead of buddying up with some revolutionaries. I also enjoy the directional combat, the different mechanics in the night and daytimes, and the general atmosphere. Our reviewer Diego was a little less enthusiastic than I, so your mileage may vary, but if you're a fan of games with choice-based stories, I highly recommend The Blood of Dawnwalker.

I like Orbitals, but I don't love it. It's an absolutely gorgeous game with visuals inspired by 80s anime and a wicked soundtrack to match. The characters are fun and charming, and even the menus are expressive and unique. The vibes are immaculate, but the actual gameplay is just okay. It's co-op only, and you'll spend its 6-hour runtime collaborating with a partner to solve puzzles and save your home space station. I just wasn't impressed with the game itself – it has some good ideas, but fails to meaningfully stand out the way similar co-op-only games do. I also don't love the story, but it's admittedly not much of a hurdle until the final moments. Despite those gripes, it's still such a joyous experience that I recommend it nonetheless. If the art style draws you in, you're in for a pretty good weekend with a friend. For my full thoughts, you can read my review here.

Friday the 13th: The Game developer IllFonic has finally made the asymmetrical horror game I’ve been wanting since playing as Jason and camp counselors, and it’s called Halloween: The Game and is out now. Kind of. IllFonic is doing the whole “pay for the more expensive edition and get early access to it” thing I hate (because it preys on FOMO and is just generally lame), so you can technically hop in right now. But if you decide to wait for the real launch, that’s next week, on September 8. Either way, I recently wrapped up its single-player campaign (IllFonic’s first) and am starting my multiplayer journey ahead of reviewing the game sometime next week. If you’re a fan of John Carpenter’s Halloween, this single-player campaign is a passionate love letter to it… but it’s also only a couple of hours long and basically a glorified tutorial for actually playing as Michael Myers in the game’s primary multiplayer experience. So, would I recommend picking this game up for just its campaign? No, absolutely not. But if you’re a fan of asymmetrical horror games, or if you’ve never tried an IllFonic joint (they’re good fun, with or without friends to join you), Halloween: The Game is shaping up to be great.

Crimson Moon has Souls-inspired combat, but it isn’t a true Soulslike. It’s actually more of a roguelike thanks to its run-based blueprint, where you embark on missions as a nephlim (a human-angel hybrid) to slay a bevy of grotesque and dangerous demons. I’m not sure entirely why – I’m sure it benefits whatever version of Earth this is – but you’ll likely not care too much because of the solid combat, a more forgiving run-based format thanks to having multiple lives, and an impressive presentation for a $20 game. While it’s not perfect, Crimson Moon offers a pretty good time, likely even more so if you rope in a friend for two-player co-op. I played the first two hours of the game on a stream this week, so be sure to check out that VOD if you want a better look at Crimson Moon in action.

en.title: Video game makers really don't want to give their customers tariff refunds
en.description: The biggest video game makers don't want to give you back your loot.
en.fullContent:
The biggest video game makers don't want to give you back your loot.

When President Donald Trump imposed sweeping tariffs by executive order last year, Sony, Microsoft, and Nintendo all raised their prices, passing those increased costs onto their customers. At the time, the companies said the price hikes were due to market conditions and the shifting economic landscape.

Now, after the US Supreme Court ruled that Trump's tariffs were illegal, forcing the administration to refund companies for tariffs they paid, those same video game makers are now arguing in court that they don't have to pass them back to their customers.

While big-box retailers like Walmart and Costco have said they intend to lower costs for consumers who were squeezed by tariff-related price hikes, the big video game makers haven't taken that route.

Attorneys for Sony Interactive Entertainment sought to dismiss a class-action lawsuit filed against the company in May. In the suit, plaintiffs said Sony charged consumers inflated prices for PlayStation consoles after the tariffs were imposed, and then sought refunds from the US government.

"They suffered no cognizable injury because they voluntarily paid the advertised prices for the consoles and received exactly what they paid for—working consoles," the attorneys said.

en.title: Orbitals Review: The Perfect Couples Co-op Game for the Switch 2
en.description: Developer Shapefarm’s debut adventure doesn’t ever really break away from its classic anime inspirations, but that might just work in its favor.
en.fullContent:
Developer Shapefarm’s debut adventure doesn’t ever really break away from its classic anime inspirations, but that might just work in its favor.

Developer Shapefarm’s debut release is more than just a stellar couch co-op adventure: Orbitals is a celebration of vintage anime that wears its inspirations on its sleeve. It’s Cowboy Bebop, Evangelion and Sailor Moon stuffed into a high-concept sci-fi story, with lovingly crafted animated cutscenes to boot. And while Orbitals never truly breaks away from these visual touchstones to blossom into a stand-alone masterpiece, it’s aping so many nearly perfect hits that the sugary nostalgia will probably be enough to keep you satiated during the game’s short playtime.

The elephant in the room is Hazelight Studios’ string of award-winning hits, like It Takes Two and Split Fiction, which have come to define the couch co-op space over the past 10 years. It’s nearly impossible not to compare similar games to Hazelight’s output, even if that seems unfair to new studios just entering the genre.

But Orbitals holds up against the best of the best — probably in no small part because its development team is helmed by ex-Hazelight talent. Orbitals Game Director Jakob Lundgren previously told Polygon that the game would integrate a lot of the Hazelight DNA, but I actually think it positively iterates on that award-winning formula in many ways.

I spent a lot of time standing around and holding down a single button to help out my partner in It Takes Two and Split Fiction. By contrast, Orbitals ensures both players are always zooming through its challenges together, making meaningful contributions to platforming sections or puzzles without lingering too long in one place.

In Orbitals, players step into the role of young space colonists, Maki and Omura, who have spent their entire lives in a stranded space colony ravaged by a mysterious radiation storm. The only thing keeping the folks on the station alive are high-tech respawn machines, named IMs, but the danger is closing in. In order to save their found family (and potentially help everyone escape the wreckage), Maki and Omura travel into the farthest reaches of space to scavenge what they need to survive.

en.title: Remote Work As A Worm, Colorful Platformers And Other New Indie Games Worth Checking Out
en.description: Plus, shipbuilding, I Am Your Beast DLC and a cat trying to stop an AI office takeover.
en.fullContent:
Plus, shipbuilding, I Am Your Beast DLC and a cat trying to stop an AI office takeover.

Welcome to our latest roundup of what's going on in the indie game space. Along with a look at some of this week's news, we'll run through some new games you can play this weekend as well as others that are a bit further out.

It's been a busy week for Double Fine Productions, which recently left Microsoft to become independent again. The studio is running an already successful Kickstarter campaign to fund a game jam, with backers getting to vote on their favorite ideas. Four of the 26 pitches will go into further development and become playable prototypes. After another round of voting, one will become a full, small-scale game.

2 Player Productions (the team behind Double Fine PsychOdyssey and other terrific documentaries) will film the process and the studio is streaming the project on Twitch to give folks an insight into development. The Kickstarter has a hell of a stretch goal too. In the unlikely event that Double Fine raises $100 million, it has promised to make Brütal Legend 2. In addition, the studio brought its previous Xbox exclusive Keeper to PS5 and dropped the price of its most recent game, Kiln, to $8.

Elsewhere, Aggro Crab is following in the footsteps of Innersloth by using much of the money it brought in from Peak to fund and publish other developers' games. It wants to help bring "intense, stylized games with an attitude" to market without being tied to any specific genres. As if I didn't like Aggro Crab enough already, developers that use generative AI slop need not apply. "I'm serious. We'll get your ass," it said.

Aggro Crab, which is only signing a couple of games per year to make sure its publishing label remains sustainable, is not demanding to recoup its entire investment from each project before developers start earning anything. "We see a lot of publishers that insist on making their money back before the developers start seeing a cent, and that just doesn't make sense to us," it said. "Revenue needs to be flowing back towards the developers so they can continue to support themselves and the games after launch."

en.title: 5 Best Video Games Like Detroit: Become Human
en.description: French game development studio Quantic Dream has been making narrative-driven video games for over 20 years. Among the studio's most popular titles...
en.fullContent:
French game development studio Quantic Dream has been making narrative-driven video games for over 20 years. Among the studio's most popular titles is the 2018 science fiction game "Detroit: Become Human," released for PlayStation 4 and PC. Set in a near-future where lifelike androids serve humanity, the game follows three different playable synthetic characters as tension between androids and humans escalates. One of the best interactive story games of all time, "Detroit: Become Human" stands as the perfect showcase for Quantic Dream's talents.

Of course, interactive story games didn't start with Quantic Dream, nor are they the only studio making them in the industry today. We're rounding up some of our favorite games that are similar to "Detroit: Become Human," each of which invites gamers to try multiple playthroughs and see the full scope of the story. Some of these games are also made by Quantic Dream, while others share similar sensibilities in storytelling and gameplay. Here are the five best video games like "Detroit: Become Human" that fans of engrossing interactive stories should try out next.

The game that introduced Quantic Dream to wider audiences was the 2010 PlayStation 3 title "Heavy Rain." A neo-noir mystery thriller, the game revolves around a serial killer known as the Origami Killer who targets young boys. When protagonist Ethan Mars' son is kidnapped by the Origami Killer, he is prepared to do anything to save his child. Gamers alternate between four different playable characters, each offering varying perspectives on the story before their paths inevitably collide.

"Heavy Rain" is the darkest and grimmest title that Quantic Dream has published to date, featuring a foreboding setting and gruesome stakes. With its multifaceted approach, this is a game that pressures players to do terrible things to advance the story as the full scope of the tale comes to light. And yet, as bleak as things get, we can't help but keep coming back to see different ways for the story to unfold. Still one of the best games that Quantic Dream has ever made, "Heavy Rain" is an atmospheric gem.

Honestly, we could've included all of Quantic Dream's games but, for the sake of variety, we're keeping it to two for this list. The other title is the studio's follow-up to "Heavy Rain": the 2013 interactive story game "Beyond: Two Souls," initially released for the PlayStation 3. The game follows protagonist Jodie Holmes, a telepath who is connected to an ethereal psychic entity known as Aiden. Players can alternate between controlling Jodie and Aiden as they progress through the story, with Jodie's abilities attracting unwanted attention from the CIA.

"Beyond: Two Souls" is one of the more peculiar Quantic Dream games, certainly since gaining mainstream attention with "Heavy Rain." The technical presentation is much more sophisticated than the studio's prior work, and Elliot Page and Willem Dafoe provide reliably good performances as their respective characters. Like "Heavy Rain," the narrative is framed like a mystery, as Jodie discovers the true nature of her backstory and Aiden's identity. This fuels the engaging nature of "Beyond: Two Souls," leading players on a twist-filled story all about human connection.
